# Equisatisfiable Not Equivalent

Two formulas are **equivalent** when they take the same value under every valuation. They are
**equisatisfiable** when one is satisfiable exactly if the other is. The second is strictly
weaker, and buying it instead of the first is what makes several standard constructions
affordable.

## Why anyone would settle for less

Converting a formula to conjunctive normal form by distributing `|` over `&` produces an
equivalent formula and can be exponentially larger. The witness is exact rather than
hypothetical: `(a₁ & b₁) | … | (aₙ & bₙ)` has precisely `2ⁿ` clauses, one per way of choosing
a side from each disjunct.

The **Tseitin encoding** gives up equivalence to escape that. Name every compound subformula
with a fresh variable, add clauses forcing the variable to equal the subformula, and assert
the top one. The result cannot be equivalent — it contains variables the original did not —
but it is satisfiable exactly when the original is, and any model of it restricted to the
original variables is a model of the original. Its size is **linear** in the input: under
sixty clauses where distribution gives 256.

That is why a SAT solver's input is never the user's formula.

## The same trade one level up

**Skolemisation** does it for quantifiers. Replacing `∃y` by a fresh function symbol applied
to the universally quantified variables in scope removes the existentials, and the result
asserts that a *specific* witness exists rather than that some witness does. The signature
changed, so equivalence is off the table; satisfiability is preserved, and refutation only
ever needed that. Every first-order resolution prover begins here.

## Why the distinction has to be stated

Both constructions are usually introduced as "converting to CNF" and "removing existentials",
phrasings that imply equivalence. A comment claiming equivalence where the construction gives
equisatisfiability is a bug in the documentation, and it is the kind that survives review
because the code is correct. In [[logic-for-computer-scientists]] the two properties are
tested differently on purpose: the CNF conversion is checked for equivalence by enumeration,
and the Tseitin encoding is checked only for preserved satisfiability plus the restriction
property — which is all it claims.

The general habit is [[counted-complexity-assertions]] applied to a semantic property rather
than a cost: state the weaker claim, and test exactly the weaker claim.
